def: Attractively unusual or old-fashioned in character or appearance.
ex: We spent the weekend exploring quaint cobblestone streets in a quiet coastal fishing village.
nat: The small bed and breakfast featured quaint antique furniture and handmade linen quilts.

mis.bad: It was a quaint of city.
mis.good: It was a quaint little town.
mis.why: Use "quaint" directly as an adjective before nouns, not followed by "of".

def: To be entitled to a particular benefit or privilege by fulfilling necessary conditions.
ex: Candidates must score above eighty percent on the technical exam to qualify for interviews.
nat: Working full-time for six months helped him qualify for company comprehensive healthcare benefits.

mis.bad: She qualifies to the scholarship.
mis.good: She qualifies for the scholarship.
mis.why: Say "qualify for [a prize/benefit]", not "qualify to".

def: Relating to, measuring, or measured by the quality of something rather than its quantity.
ex: User interviews provide invaluable qualitative feedback that pure numeric telemetry simply cannot capture.
nat: The market study combined qualitative customer impressions with rigorous quantitative financial modeling.

mis.bad: We need qualitative data numbers.
mis.good: We need qualitative user insights.
mis.why: Do not confuse "qualitative" (descriptive qualities) with "quantitative" (measurable numbers).

def: Relating to, measuring, or measured by the quantity of something rather than quality.
ex: Our engineering team relies heavily on quantitative metrics like page load times and error rates.
nat: Quantitative analysis helps portfolio managers evaluate investment risk without emotional bias.

mis.bad: The report gave a quantitative of the errors.
mis.good: The report gave quantitative data on errors.
mis.why: Use "quantitative" as an adjective ("quantitative analysis"), not a noun.

def: Relating to quantum mechanics; or denoting a huge, sudden advance or change.
ex: The discovery represented a quantum leap forward in our understanding of superconducting materials.
nat: Researchers are developing quantum computers that can solve complex cryptography problems in seconds.

mis.bad: It was a quantum jump very small.
mis.good: It was a quantum leap forward.
mis.why: "Quantum leap" in modern idiom means a huge, sudden breakthrough, not a small step.

def: A heated argument or disagreement, typically about a trivial matter.
ex: The co-founders had a bitter quarrel over product equity and decided to part ways.
nat: I have no quarrel with your conclusion, though I disagree with your methodology.

mis.bad: They had a quarrel about the money yesterday.
mis.good: They had a quarrel over money yesterday.
mis.why: Use "quarrel over/about [a topic]", typically with "have a quarrel with [someone]".

def: A place from which stone or other materials are extracted, or an animal being hunted.
ex: Blocks of white marble were transported directly from the hillside quarry to the cathedral.
nat: The predator stalked its unsuspecting quarry through the dense overgrown jungle brush.

mis.bad: The stone was mined in a quary.
mis.good: The stone was extracted from a quarry.
mis.why: Spell "quarry" with double "r".

def: Done, produced, or occurring once every quarter of a year.
ex: The board convenes every three months to review quarterly earnings and approve department budgets.
nat: Subscribe to our quarterly research journal to stay updated on distributed system trends.

mis.bad: We have a quarterly meeting every month.
mis.good: We have a quarterly meeting every three months.
mis.why: "Quarterly" means every three months (four times a year), not monthly or four times a month.

def: To satisfy one's thirst by drinking; or extinguish a fire.
ex: Drinking ice-cold coconut water after a five-kilometer run quickly quenches your summer thirst.
nat: Firefighters worked tirelessly through the night to quench the lingering warehouse blaze.

mis.bad: I drank water to kill my thirst.
mis.good: I drank cold water to quench my thirst.
mis.why: In Portuguese you "mata a sede"; in natural English you "quench your thirst".

def: A long or arduous search for something valuable or meaningful.
ex: His lifelong quest for truth inspired generations of investigative journalists across the country.
nat: The startup launched a bold quest to build affordable zero-emission commercial aircraft.

mis.bad: He is in a quest for knowledges.
mis.good: He is on a quest for knowledge.
mis.why: Say "on a quest for knowledge" (uncountable "knowledge", preposition "on").

def: Doubtful as regards truth, validity, honesty, or morality.
ex: The company accounting practices came under heavy scrutiny after questionable offshore transfers surfaced.
nat: It is highly questionable whether adding another microservice will actually solve our latency problem.

mis.bad: His decision was very questionary.
mis.good: His decision was highly questionable.
mis.why: Do not confuse "questionable" (duvidoso) with "questionnaire" (questionário).

pt: esperto / perspicaz e rápido de raciocínio
def: Able to think and respond quickly, cleverly, and humorously in unexpected situations.
ex: A quick-witted moderator kept the panel discussion entertaining despite heated disagreements among guests.
nat: Her quick-witted response defused the tense atmosphere in the client boardroom instantly.

mis.bad: He is a very quick-wit person.
mis.good: He is a very quick-witted person.
mis.why: Use the hyphenated adjective "quick-witted", not the noun "quick-wit".

def: At a fast speed; rapidly; or in a comparatively short time.
ex: Engineers moved quickly to patch the vulnerability before attackers could exploit public endpoints.
nat: She adapted quickly to working across European and Pacific time zones from home.

mis.bad: He ran very quick to catch the train.
mis.good: He ran very quickly to catch the train.
mis.why: In careful English, modify verbs with the adverb "quickly", not the adjective "quick".

def: The state or quality of being quiet; calmness or stillness.
ex: She cherished the early morning quietness before her children woke up for school.
nat: The library strict quietness policy helped students concentrate on preparing for medical exams.

mis.bad: I love the quiet of the morning.
mis.good: I love the quietness of the morning.
mis.why: While "the quiet" is common colloquially, "quietness" is the formal abstract noun.

def: A peculiar behavioral habit or an unexpected twist in a system.
ex: Every programming language has its own strange syntactic quirks that beginners must memorize.
nat: One endearing quirk of his personality is humming quietly whenever deep in thought.

mis.bad: That is a strange cork of him.
mis.good: That is a strange quirk of his.
mis.why: Do not confuse "quirk" (peculiaridade) with "cork" (rolha de garrafa).

def: Characterized by peculiar, unconventional, or unexpected traits that are often charming.
ex: The boutique hotel gained popularity online thanks to its quirky retro room designs.
nat: She has a quirky sense of humor that makes everyone on the team smile.

mis.bad: He has a very corky personality.
mis.good: He has a very quirky personality.
mis.why: Spell "quirky" with "qu-i-r-k-y".

def: To stop doing something, or officially leave a job or school.
ex: He decided to quit his corporate consulting job and pursue a software career.
nat: Doctors advised him to quit smoking immediately to improve his cardiovascular health.

mis.bad: He quitted his job last month.
mis.good: He quit his job last month.
mis.why: In modern American English, the past tense of "quit" is "quit", not "quitted".

def: To tremble or shake with a slight, rapid, vibrating motion.
ex: Her voice began to quiver with suppressed emotion as she accepted the lifetime award.
nat: Dry autumn leaves quiver gently in the chilly October breeze along the lake.

mis.bad: His hands were quivering from cold.
mis.good: His hands were shivering from the cold.
mis.why: Use "shiver" for cold; "quiver" is typically used for subtle emotional vibration or nervous excitement.

def: The minimum number of members of an assembly or society that must be present.
ex: The committee could not vote on the budget because they lacked an official quorum.
nat: Shareholders waited thirty minutes until enough proxy votes arrived to establish a legal quorum.

mis.bad: We did not have quorum to vote.
mis.good: We did not have a quorum to vote.
mis.why: In English, use the indefinite article: "have a quorum".

def: A limited or fixed number or amount of people or things permitted or demanded.
ex: Sales representatives must hit their quarterly revenue quota to qualify for year-end bonuses.
nat: The European Union establishes strict fishing quotas to protect dwindling Atlantic cod populations.

mis.bad: He filled his quota of sellings.
mis.good: He met his sales quota.
mis.why: Say "meet / exceed a sales quota", not "fill a quota of sellings".

def: A group of words taken from a text or speech, or a formal price estimate.
ex: Please send us an official written quotation for the cloud database migration services.
nat: The author opened every single chapter with an inspirational quotation from ancient Greek philosophers.

mis.bad: Can you give me a quotation of price?
mis.good: Can you provide a price quotation?
mis.why: Use "price quotation" or simply "quote/estimate".

def: The action of waiting in a line or queue, or managing tasks in sequence.
ex: Modern distributed message systems rely on reliable task queueing to process millions of transactions.
nat: Commuters were frustrated by hours of slow queueing outside the international terminal security gates.

mis.bad: The queueing of the customers was long.
mis.good: The customer queue was long.
mis.why: Use "the queue" for the physical line, reserving "queueing" for the process or mechanism.

def: Shining or glowing brightly; emanating joy, love, or good health.
ex: The bride looked radiant as she walked down the aisle surrounded by smiling guests.
nat: Sunflowers turn their radiant yellow faces toward the morning sun in open fields.

mis.bad: She was radiant of happiness.
mis.good: She was radiant with happiness.
mis.why: The correct preposition is "radiant with [joy/happiness]", not "of".

def: To emit energy, especially light or heat, in the form of rays or waves.
ex: The dark asphalt street continues to radiate stored solar heat long after sunset.
nat: Leaders who radiate calm confidence help keep their teams productive during operational crises.

mis.bad: The fire radiated out heat.
mis.good: The fire radiated heat.
mis.why: "Radiate" is directly transitive when governing an emitted substance; omit "out".

def: Relating to or affecting the fundamental nature of something; far-reaching or thorough.
ex: Adopting a four-day work week was a radical departure from traditional corporate schedules.
nat: The team proposed radical changes to the database architecture to eliminate ongoing deadlocks.

mis.bad: He had a radical approach of the problem.
mis.good: He had a radical approach to the problem.
mis.why: Use "approach to [a problem]", not "of".

def: A straight line from the center to the circumference of a circle or sphere.
ex: There are three excellent specialty coffee shops within a five-block radius of our office.
nat: Measure the circle radius before applying the standard area formula in your code.

mis.bad: The radius from the circle is five meters.
mis.good: The radius of the circle is five meters.
mis.why: Say "radius of a circle", not "radius from".

def: A sudden surprise attack, or a rapid search by police or tax inspectors.
ex: Federal police conducted an early morning raid on the warehouse containing smuggled electronic goods.
nat: Corporate rivals launched a raid to hire away our three top computer vision researchers.

mis.bad: Police made a raid on the office.
mis.good: Police carried out a raid on the office.
mis.why: Use "carry out / conduct a raid", not "make a raid".

def: A consequence of an action or event, especially when complex or unwelcome.
ex: Executives failed to consider the legal ramifications of storing European user data outside Frankfurt.
nat: The geopolitical crisis has profound ramifications for global crude oil and agricultural trade.

mis.bad: This decision has many ramifications for we.
mis.good: This decision has many ramifications for us.
mis.why: After the preposition "for", use the object pronoun "us", not the subject pronoun "we".

def: Without definite aim, reason, or pattern; in a random manner.
ex: The testing script randomly selects one thousand records from the customer database for validation.
nat: Participants were randomly assigned to either the experimental drug group or the placebo.

mis.bad: The items were chosen at randomly.
mis.good: The items were chosen at random / randomly.
mis.why: Say either "randomly" or the prepositional phrase "at random", never "at randomly".

def: A person entrusted with the protection and preservation of a park or forest.
ex: The park ranger warned hikers not to leave food scraps outside their camping tents.
nat: She worked two summers as a seasonal forest ranger in Yosemite National Park.

mis.bad: The ranger of the park guided us.
mis.good: The park ranger guided us.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "park ranger" rather than "ranger of the park".

def: To give a specified position on a scale, or hold a particular position.
ex: Independent reviewers rank our customer support as the most responsive in the entire industry.
nat: Brazil ranks among the world top exporters of soybeans and specialty arabica coffee beans.

mis.bad: Our company is ranked like the best.
mis.good: Our company is ranked as the best.
mis.why: Use "rank as [something]", not "rank like".

def: A sum of money demanded or paid for the release of a captive or data.
ex: The hospital refused to pay the cryptocurrency ransom demanded by the international cyber gang.
nat: Kidnappers demanded five million dollars in ransom before releasing the captured shipping vessel.

mis.bad: They paid a ransom to release of the files.
mis.good: They paid a ransom to release the files.
mis.why: Use "to release [object]" without the preposition "of".

def: Happening in a short time or at a great rate; fast.
ex: The company experienced rapid customer growth after its launch on a popular product portal.
nat: Take rapid action if you notice unauthorized login attempts on your primary banking account.

mis.bad: He made a rapid run to the bus.
mis.good: He ran quickly to catch the bus.
mis.why: In natural English, use adverbs like "quickly" with action verbs rather than "made a rapid run".

def: Very quickly; at a great rate.
ex: The floodwaters rose rapidly after three continuous days of torrential summer rainfall.
nat: Electric vehicle adoption is spreading rapidly across major European and North American metropolitan areas.

mis.bad: The technology is developing in a rapidly way.
mis.good: The technology is developing rapidly.
mis.why: Use the adverb "rapidly" alone, avoiding the wordy calque "in a rapidly way".

def: Based on or in accordance with reason or logic.
ex: Try to make a rational financial decision rather than reacting impulsively to market panics.
nat: There must be a rational explanation for why the server rebooted in the night.

mis.bad: He gave a reason rational.
mis.good: He gave a rational explanation.
mis.why: Place adjectives before the noun in English: "rational explanation", not "reason rational".

def: A set of reasons or a logical basis for a course of action.
ex: The lead architect explained the rationale behind migrating from microservices back to a monolith.
nat: What was the business rationale for canceling the most anticipated feature of the year?

mis.bad: The rational behind this choice is clear.
mis.good: The rationale behind this choice is clear.
mis.why: Spell the noun with an "e" at the end: "rationale" (justification) vs. "rational" (logical).

def: To attempt to explain or justify behavior or an attitude with logical reasons.
ex: He tried to rationalize skipping daily exercise by claiming he had no spare time.
nat: The CFO moved to rationalize operations by consolidating three regional distribution fulfillment centers.

mis.bad: She rationalized for why she was late.
mis.good: She rationalized why she was late.
mis.why: "Rationalize" does not need "for"; say "rationalize why/that...".

def: The state of being fully prepared for something, or willingness to do something.
ex: The engineering team conducted a disaster recovery drill to evaluate operational system readiness.
nat: She expressed her complete readiness to take on additional technical leadership responsibilities.

mis.bad: Our ready was confirmed by the boss.
mis.good: Our readiness was confirmed by the boss.
mis.why: Use the noun "readiness", not the adjective "ready", as the subject or object.

def: The attitude or practice of accepting a situation as it is and dealing with it.
ex: A healthy dose of realism is needed when estimating software delivery deadlines for clients.
nat: Nineteenth-century literary realism depicted everyday working-class struggles with unflinching and painful accuracy.

mis.bad: He showed much realist in his planning.
mis.good: He showed great realism in his planning.
mis.why: Use the noun "realism" for the quality, reserving "realist" for the person.

def: Having or showing a sensible and practical idea of what can be achieved.
ex: Setting a realistic daily study habit of twenty minutes is better than ambitious burnout.
nat: The video game graphics were so realistic that players felt truly immersed in combat.

mis.bad: We need a plan more realistic.
mis.good: We need a more realistic plan.
mis.why: Adjectives go before the noun: "a more realistic plan".

def: A kingdom, or a field or domain of activity, interest, or thought.
ex: Generative artificial intelligence has expanded possibilities within the realm of digital art creation.
nat: Quantum computing moves complex encryption problems out of the realm of human intuition.

mis.bad: This is outside the realm from science.
mis.good: This is outside the realm of science.
mis.why: Always use "realm of [a field/topic]", never "from".

def: To state again strongly, or confirm the validity of a previous agreement.
ex: The company board issued a statement to reaffirm their commitment to renewable carbon targets.
nat: Both leaders met in Geneva to reaffirm their longstanding mutual security defense treaty.

mis.bad: He reaffirmed about his decision.
mis.good: He reaffirmed his decision.
mis.why: "Reaffirm" is transitive; do not insert "about".

def: To change the position, time, or order of something.
ex: Can we rearrange our weekly one-on-one meeting to Thursday afternoon instead of Tuesday?
nat: She decided to rearrange the living room furniture to create space for an easel.

mis.bad: We must to rearrange the date.
mis.good: We must rearrange the date.
mis.why: Modal verbs like "must" take the bare infinitive without "to": "must rearrange".

def: An act of violent or open resistance to an established government or ruler.
ex: The harsh new tax prompted a widespread rebellion among merchants in the capital city.
nat: Teenage rebellion often manifests as unconventional fashion choices and challenging established family traditions.

mis.bad: The soldiers made a rebellion.
mis.good: The soldiers staged a rebellion.
mis.why: Use verbs like "stage", "lead", or "crush a rebellion", not "make a rebellion".

def: To build something again after it has been damaged or destroyed; reconstruct.
ex: Communities banded together to rebuild their coastal village after the destructive hurricane struck.
nat: The team had to rebuild the frontend architecture completely from scratch last quarter.

mis.bad: They rebuilded the database yesterday.
mis.good: They rebuilt the database yesterday.
mis.why: The irregular past tense and past participle of "rebuild" is "rebuilt", not "rebuilded".

def: To express sharp disapproval or criticism of someone because of their behavior.
ex: The manager publicly rebuked the senior engineer for ignoring mandatory code review guidelines.
nat: She felt hurt when the professor rebuked her for arriving five minutes late.

mis.bad: He rebuked to his son.
mis.good: He rebuked his son.
mis.why: "Rebuke" takes a direct personal object without "to".

def: To calculate something again, especially when conditions or input variables have changed.
ex: The GPS navigation app will automatically recalculate your route when you miss an exit.
nat: We need to recalculate our quarterly revenue projections after the unexpected contract loss.

mis.bad: The system recalculates of the score.
mis.good: The system recalculates the score.
mis.why: "Recalculate" is directly transitive; drop "of".

def: The part of a telephone you hold to your ear; or person/device receiving.
ex: She lifted the telephone receiver and dialed the local emergency helpline immediately.
nat: Make sure the wireless audio receiver is plugged securely into the laptop USB port.

mis.bad: Pick up the receptor of the phone.
mis.good: Pick up the telephone receiver.
mis.why: Do not say "receptor" for a telephone handset; use "receiver".

def: A person or thing that receives something such as an award, email, or parcel.
ex: Double-check that every email recipient on the confidential distribution list is authorized to view.
nat: The Nobel Peace Prize recipient delivered a moving speech on human rights education.

mis.bad: The email was sent to the destined.
mis.good: The email was sent to the intended recipient.
mis.why: Calque alert: "destinatário" in Portuguese is "recipient" or "addressee" in English, never "destined".

def: Without thinking or caring about the consequences of an action; careless of danger.
ex: Driving at excessive speeds in dense fog is an extremely reckless and dangerous behavior.
nat: The financial firm collapsed after executives engaged in reckless speculative derivatives trading overseas.

mis.bad: He was reckless with his money (meaning rich).
mis.good: He was careless / reckless with his money.
mis.why: Make sure you understand "reckless" means dangerously irresponsible, not generous.

def: To retrieve or recover something previously lost, given, or taken away.
ex: Passengers must present their baggage claim ticket to reclaim lost luggage at customs.
nat: The city launched an ambitious environmental initiative to reclaim abandoned industrial waterfront zones.

mis.bad: He reclaimed about his rights.
mis.good: He reclaimed his rights.
mis.why: "Reclaim" takes a direct object without prepositions like "about".

def: The action or faculty of remembering something, or a memory itself.
ex: To the best of my recollection, the security update was scheduled for Thursday.
nat: She had only a hazy childhood recollection of living in the countryside.
col: to the best of my recollection

mis.bad: I have no recollection about the incident.
mis.good: I have no recollection of the incident.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "recollection of [something]", not "about".

def: Compensation or reward given for loss, injury, or harm suffered.
ex: The airline provided hotel vouchers and cash recompense for the canceled transatlantic flight.
nat: He dedicated his life to community service without ever seeking personal financial recompense.

mis.bad: He received a recompensation for his loss.
mis.good: He received recompense for his loss.
mis.why: The standard noun is "recompense" or "compensation", not "recompensation".

def: To consider something again, especially with a possibility of changing one's decision.
ex: We kindly urge the client to reconsider their decision to cancel the contract.
nat: Taking a long walk in the fresh air prompted him to reconsider his resignation.

mis.bad: I will reconsider about your proposal.
mis.good: I will reconsider your proposal.
mis.why: "Reconsider" is transitive; do not insert "about".

def: The action of considering something again, especially with a view to change.
ex: The dismissed employee submitted a formal request for reconsideration to the human resources panel.
nat: The committee agreed that the municipal zoning proposal merited further careful reconsideration.

mis.bad: We ask for a reconsideration about this.
mis.good: We ask for reconsideration of this matter.
mis.why: Say "reconsideration of [a matter]", not "about".

def: To tell someone about something, giving a detailed account of an event.
ex: The elderly survivor began to recount memories of escaping through the alpine mountain pass.
nat: In his keynote address, the founder recounted the chaotic early days of the company.

mis.bad: He recounted about his trip to Paris.
mis.good: He recounted his trip to Paris.
mis.why: "Recount" is directly transitive; omit "about".

def: To create something again, or reproduce a past event or environment.
ex: Software engineers must recreate the bug locally before attempting to write a permanent patch.
nat: The historical museum recreated an authentic nineteenth-century Victorian apothecary shop inside its gallery.

mis.bad: Can you recreate of the error?
mis.good: Can you recreate the error?
mis.why: "Recreate" is directly transitive; drop the preposition "of".

def: Occurring often or repeatedly; happening again and again.
ex: He scheduled an appointment with a neurologist to investigate recurrent debilitating migraine headaches.
nat: A recurrent theme throughout her research papers is the impact of sleep on memory.

mis.bad: This is a recurrant issue in our code.
mis.good: This is a recurrent issue in our code.
mis.why: Spell "recurrent" with "ent" at the end, not "ant".

def: Occurring repeatedly or at regular intervals, especially billing or events.
ex: Setting up a monthly recurring payment ensures your web hosting domain never expires unexpectedly.
nat: Nightmares about missing college exams were a recurring dream throughout his twenties.

mis.bad: We pay a recurred fee every month.
mis.good: We pay a recurring fee every month.
mis.why: Use the present participle adjective "recurring", not the past participle "recurred".

def: The process of defining a function or problem in terms of itself.
ex: Using deep recursion without a proper base case will inevitably cause a stack overflow.
nat: Understanding tree traversal algorithms requires a firm grasp of both iteration and recursion.

mis.bad: The function uses recursivity.
mis.good: The function uses recursion.
mis.why: In standard English computer science, use "recursion", not the calque "recursivity".

def: To compensate for faults, or exchange goods/vouchers for cash or prizes.
ex: Frequent flyer passengers can redeem airline reward miles for free domestic round-trip tickets.
nat: He worked hard to redeem his professional reputation after the costly project failure.

mis.bad: I redeemed my points for get a flight.
mis.good: I redeemed my points to get a flight.
mis.why: Use "to get", not "for get" (calque of Portuguese "para pegar").

def: The action of saving or being saved from error, or exchanging a voucher.
ex: The voucher allows a single redemption per customer at participating retail branch locations.
nat: The fallen athlete found moral redemption by coaching underprivileged youth in his hometown.

mis.bad: He is beyond of redemption.
mis.good: He is beyond redemption.
mis.why: The idiom is "beyond redemption", without the preposition "of".

def: To distribute something again or differently, especially wealth, resources, or tasks.
ex: The load balancer will automatically redistribute incoming network connections across healthy web servers.
nat: Progressive tax policies aim to redistribute national wealth to fund public school systems.

mis.bad: We redistributed the tasks between everyone.
mis.good: We redistributed the tasks among everyone.
mis.why: Use "among" when distributing between more than two people or entities.

def: The use of a source of information, or a letter recommending someone.
ex: Candidates should provide at least two professional references from previous engineering leadership roles.
nat: Keep this technical cheat sheet nearby for quick reference while writing backend queries.

mis.bad: I gave his name like a reference.
mis.good: I gave his name as a reference.
mis.why: Say "as a reference", never "like a reference".

def: Purified or free from impurities, or elegant and polished in taste.
ex: After weeks of usability testing, the product designer presented a remarkably refined interface mockup.
nat: Nutritionists advise limiting intake of refined sugars and processed white flour in diets.

mis.bad: He has a very refinery manner.
mis.good: He has very refined manners.
mis.why: Use the adjective "refined", reserving "refinery" for an industrial processing plant.

def: An industrial installation where a substance is refined into finished commercial products.
ex: The coastal oil refinery processes over two hundred thousand barrels of crude daily.
nat: Air quality near the chemical refinery improved following stricter environmental municipal regulations.

mis.bad: The oil refinaria had an explosion.
mis.good: The oil refinery had an explosion.
mis.why: Remember "refinery" is the English term for "refinaria".

def: Providing a reflection of light, or characterized by deep thought and meditation.
ex: Night joggers should always wear bright clothing equipped with high-visibility reflective safety strips.
nat: Writing daily in a private journal encourages a calm and deeply reflective mindset.

mis.bad: He was in a reflexing mood.
mis.good: He was in a reflective mood.
mis.why: Use "reflective" to describe thoughtful moods, not "reflexing".

def: To stop oneself from doing something; hold back voluntarily.
ex: Please refrain from taking flash photographs during the classical symphony orchestra performance.
nat: She had to refrain from correcting her manager pronunciation during the client call.

mis.bad: Please refrain to smoke here.
mis.good: Please refrain from smoking here.
mis.why: Always use "refrain from + -ing", never "refrain to + verb".

def: To give new strength or energy to, or reload a web page.
ex: If the analytics dashboard does not update automatically, refresh your web browser tab.
nat: A cold shower on a humid summer afternoon will instantly refresh your energy.

mis.bad: I refreshed on the page.
mis.good: I refreshed the page.
mis.why: "Refresh" is directly transitive in computing contexts; omit "on".

def: Light snacks and drinks served at a meeting, party, or during travel.
ex: Light refreshments including fruit skewers and herbal tea will be served after presentations.
nat: A brisk stroll through the pine forest brought mental refreshment after long exams.

mis.bad: We bought many refreshments for drink.
mis.good: Light refreshments were served.
mis.why: When referring to snacks and drinks, "refreshments" is typically plural.

def: Without paying attention to the present situation; in spite of everything.
ex: The outdoor marathon will take place on Sunday morning regardless of the weather.
nat: We decided to release the patch today regardless of minor cosmetic UI defects.

mis.bad: Irregardless of what he says, we go.
mis.good: Regardless of what he says, we are going.
mis.why: Avoid the non-standard word "irregardless"; use "regardless".

def: A government, especially an authoritarian one, or an organized system or routine.
ex: The authoritarian military regime restricted freedom of assembly and strictly monitored internet activity.
nat: Following a strict daily sleep regime helped the executive recover from burnout.

mis.bad: I am doing a regime to lose weight.
mis.good: I am on a diet to lose weight.
mis.why: False friend alert: for losing weight, use "diet", not "regime" (which refers to political rule or health routines).

def: Relating to or characteristic of a particular region, district, or area.
ex: The company launched a targeted marketing campaign tailored specifically for regional southern dialects.
nat: Regional trains between small European towns offer scenic and relaxing daily travel experiences.

mis.bad: He works at the region office.
mis.good: He works at the regional office.
mis.why: Use the adjective "regional" before the noun "office", not the noun "region".

def: The action or process of registering or of being registered.
ex: Online registration for the annual international developer conference closes at midnight on Friday.
nat: Make sure to bring your vehicle registration documents when visiting the inspection center.

mis.bad: I finished my register for the course.
mis.good: I finished my registration for the course.
mis.why: Use the noun "registration" for enrollment, reserving "register" as a verb or official record book.

def: To control or maintain the rate or speed of a machine or process.
ex: Independent government agencies regulate financial markets to prevent insider trading and consumer fraud.
nat: The body sweating mechanism helps regulate core internal temperature during strenuous physical exercise.

mis.bad: The law regulates about emissions.
mis.good: The law regulates emissions.
mis.why: "Regulate" is a transitive verb; omit "about".

def: A person or body that supervises a particular industry or business activity.
ex: Federal aviation regulators ordered immediate safety inspections for that specific aircraft engine model.
nat: Adjust the pressure regulator on the gas canister before lighting the camping stove.

mis.bad: The company was fined by the regulamentator.
mis.good: The company was fined by the regulator.
mis.why: The English noun is "regulator", not "regulamentator".

def: To hold royal office; or to be the dominant feature or aspect.
ex: Queen Victoria reigned over the British Empire for sixty-three remarkable and transformative years.
nat: Confusion reigned in the server room when all primary networking monitors went black.

mis.bad: The king reined for forty years.
mis.good: The king reigned for forty years.
mis.why: Do not confuse "reign" (reinar) with "rein" (rédea) or "rain" (chuva), though all sound identical /reɪn/.

def: To dismiss as inadequate, inappropriate, or not to one's taste.
ex: The review committee had to reject the grant proposal due to budgetary constraints.
nat: Her body did not reject the transplanted kidney thanks to immunosuppressive medications.

mis.bad: He rejected to sign the paper.
mis.good: He refused to sign the paper.
mis.why: Use "refuse + to + verb", but use "reject + direct noun object" ("reject the offer").

def: To feel or show great joy or delight about an event or achievement.
ex: Fans rejoiced across the city when their home football club won the championship.
nat: We have good reason to rejoice after concluding six months of grueling negotiations.

mis.bad: They rejoiced with the victory.
mis.good: They rejoiced at the victory / rejoiced in the victory.
mis.why: Use "rejoice at/in [an event/news]", not "with".

def: To make someone or something look or feel younger, fresher, or more lively.
ex: Taking a full weekend off away from screens will rejuvenate your creative energy.
nat: The municipal council invested millions to rejuvenate the historic downtown shopping commercial district.

mis.bad: The vacation rejuvenated to me.
mis.good: The vacation rejuvenated me.
mis.why: "Rejuvenate" takes a direct personal object without "to".

def: To relight a fire, or revive something lost like a feeling or interest.
ex: Meeting after ten years helped them rekindle their old college friendship almost immediately.
nat: Reading science fiction novels as an adult helped rekindle his childhood love of astronomy.

mis.bad: They rekindled up their friendship.
mis.good: They rekindled their friendship.
mis.why: Do not add "up" to "rekindle"; it is directly transitive.

def: To make or show a connection between, or feel sympathy or understanding.
ex: Many young developers can relate to the feeling of imposter syndrome during onboarding.
nat: The research paper attempts to relate daily caffeine consumption to chronic sleep quality.

mis.bad: I can relate with your problem.
mis.good: I can relate to your problem.
mis.why: When meaning empathize or understand, the standard idiom is "relate to", not "with".

def: Oppressively constant; incessant; unyielding in severity or determination.
ex: The startup succeeded through relentless execution and obsessive attention to daily customer feedback.
nat: Relentless heavy rain caused multiple landslides along the mountainous coastal highway overnight.

mis.bad: He was relentless to stop.
mis.good: He was relentless in his pursuit.
mis.why: Use "relentless in [noun/pursuit]", not "relentless to + verb".

def: Dependence on or trust in someone or something for support or function.
ex: Our heavy reliance on a single cloud vendor poses a significant operational risk.
nat: Modern agriculture excessive reliance on chemical pesticides can damage delicate regional bee populations.

mis.bad: Our reliance in this server is risky.
mis.good: Our reliance on this server is risky.
mis.why: Always use "reliance on [something]", never "in".

def: An object surviving from an earlier time, especially one of historical interest.
ex: The ancient bronze coin proved to be an authentic relic from Roman times.
nat: Sending official memos by paper fax feels like a hilarious technological relic today.

mis.bad: It is an historical relic.
mis.good: It is a historical relic.
mis.why: Use "a historical" in standard American English, as "historical" begins with a pronounced /h/ sound.

def: To cause pain, distress, or difficulty to become less severe; replace someone on duty.
ex: Taking regular walking breaks will relieve tension in your neck and lower back.
nat: The night shift security guard arrived at six to relieve his daytime colleague.

mis.bad: This medicine relieves of the headache.
mis.good: This medicine relieves the headache.
mis.why: "Relieve" is a transitive verb; do not add "of" after it when referring to pain.

def: To enjoy greatly; take immense pleasure in doing something.
ex: Great problem solvers relish the challenge of debugging obscure distributed race conditions.
nat: She relished every moment of her three-month sabbatical traveling across South America.

mis.bad: I relish to speak in public.
mis.good: I relish speaking in public.
mis.why: "Relish" is followed by a gerund (-ing) or a noun phrase, never an infinitive with "to".

def: A part, number, or quantity that is left over after other parts have been removed.
ex: She spent the remainder of the afternoon reviewing customer feedback and responding to emails.
nat: Divide fourteen by four and the resulting mathematical remainder is exactly two.

mis.bad: The remain of the team agreed.
mis.good: The remainder of the team agreed.
mis.why: Use "remainder" or "rest" as a noun, not "remain" (which is primarily a verb).

def: A small remaining quantity of something, especially after the greater part has gone.
ex: Tourists can still see ancient stone remnants of the Roman city defensive wall.
nat: Only small remnants of the original virgin rainforest survive in this developed province.

mis.bad: These are remnants from the past.
mis.good: These are remnants of the past.
mis.why: Say "remnants of [something]", not "from".

def: Situated far from the main centers of population; distant; or slight.
ex: They rented a quiet cabin in a remote mountain valley without cellular reception.
nat: There is only a remote chance that the legacy server recovers without restoration.

mis.bad: I work in a remote way.
mis.good: I work remotely / have a remote job.
mis.why: Use the adverb "remotely" or the compound "remote work", not "in a remote way".

pt: remotamente / à distância / nem de longe
def: From a distance; without physical presence; or in the slightest degree.
ex: More than half of our software engineering team works remotely from five continents.
nat: His latest excuse for missing the sprint retrospective was not even remotely plausible.

mis.bad: I work from remote.
mis.good: I work remotely.
mis.why: Do not say "work from remote"; use the adverb "remotely" or say "work from home".

def: To give a new name to someone or something.
ex: Please rename the image file before uploading it to the product asset server.
nat: The company chose to rename its flagship product to appeal to younger audiences.

mis.bad: Rename the file with new name.
mis.good: Rename the file to the new name.
mis.why: Use "rename something to [new name]", not "with".

def: To formally declare one's abandonment of a claim, right, possession, or belief.
ex: The royal prince decided to renounce his rights to the throne for love.
nat: Several rebel leaders agreed to renounce violence and join constitutional political peace talks.

mis.bad: He renounced to his inheritance.
mis.good: He renounced his inheritance.
mis.why: "Renounce" is directly transitive in English; do not add "to" (calque of "renunciar a").

def: The action of renovating a building or structure; repairing and modernizing.
ex: The municipal public library will remain closed during autumn for comprehensive seismic renovations.
nat: Kitchen renovations often cost significantly more than homeowners initially budget for their properties.

mis.bad: The office is making a reform.
mis.good: The office is undergoing renovations.
mis.why: False friend alert: "reforma de prédio" is "renovation" or "refurbishment", not "reform" (which refers to political/social change).

def: Known or talked about by many people; famous and widely respected.
ex: The university invited a world-renowned theoretical physicist to deliver the commencement keynote address.
nat: Naples is internationally renowned for producing the crispiest authentic wood-fired sourdough pizza.

mis.bad: He is renowned by his discoveries.
mis.good: He is renowned for his discoveries.
mis.why: Say "renowned for [an achievement/quality]", never "by".

def: To revoke or annul a law or parliamentary act by official vote.
ex: Parliament voted overwhelmingly to repeal the archaic seventeenth-century maritime commerce tariff law.
nat: Civil rights advocates spent decades lobbying legislators to repeal discriminatory municipal voting ordinances.

mis.bad: They repealed off the tax.
mis.good: They repealed the tax.
mis.why: "Repeal" takes a direct object without particles like "off" or "down".

def: To say or do something again, or happen several times.
ex: Could you please repeat your question more slowly so everyone can understand clearly?
nat: Mistakes happen in engineering, but we must never repeat the exact same deployment error.

mis.bad: He repeated again what he said.
mis.good: He repeated what he said.
mis.why: Saying "repeat again" is redundant because "repeat" already includes the meaning of "again".

def: To drive back an attack, or push away through force or disgust.
ex: Natural citronella oil helps repel mosquitoes and ticks during evening summer camping trips.
nat: Like magnetic poles repel each other while opposite magnetic poles attract each other.

mis.bad: Magnets repel against each other.
mis.good: Magnets repel each other.
mis.why: "Repel" is directly transitive; do not insert "against".

def: To feel or express sincere regret or remorse about one's wrongdoing.
ex: The criminal showed genuine remorse and asked for forgiveness to repent for his deeds.
nat: It is never too late to repent and build honest relationships with loved ones.

mis.bad: I repent of having bought that car.
mis.good: I regret buying that car.
mis.why: "Repent" has strong religious or moral connotations of atoning for sin; for daily decisions, use "regret".

def: The action of repeating something that has already been said or done.
ex: Spaced repetition is one of the most effective techniques for long-term vocabulary retention.
nat: His speech suffered from tedious repetition and lacked concrete proposals for the listeners.

mis.bad: Learning requires many repetitions.
mis.good: Learning requires frequent repetition.
mis.why: "Repetition" is often used uncountably when referring to practice or review.

def: Containing or characterized by repetition, especially when tedious or boring.
ex: Automating repetitive manual database backup tasks freed up significant time for core feature development.
nat: Factory assembly work can cause painful physical repetitive strain injuries over several years.

mis.bad: The work was very repetitious.
mis.good: The work was very repetitive.
mis.why: While "repetitious" exists, "repetitive" is the standard modern word for boring repeated tasks.

def: To take the place of, or provide a substitute for someone or something.
ex: The engineering team plans to replace the legacy monolith with lightweight modern event-driven microservices.
nat: Remember to replace the vehicle cabin air filter at least once every twelve months.

mis.bad: We replaced the old server for a new one.
mis.good: We replaced the old server with a new one.
mis.why: The standard collocation is "replace X with Y", not "for".

def: To fill something up again; restore to a former level or condition.
ex: Drink plenty of electrolyte water to replenish lost fluids after a grueling marathon race.
nat: The warehouse team worked overtime to replenish retail shelves before the holiday shopping rush.

mis.bad: We need to replenish of our stock.
mis.good: We need to replenish our stock.
mis.why: "Replenish" takes a direct object without the preposition "of".

def: To make an exact copy of; or reproduce experimental results consistently.
ex: Other independent laboratories were completely unable to replicate the controversial cold fusion experimental findings.
nat: Distributed databases replicate committed write operations across three geographically separated availability zones.

mis.bad: Can you replicate with the experiment?
mis.good: Can you replicate the experiment?
mis.why: "Replicate" is directly transitive; omit "with".

def: An account given of a particular matter, especially after thorough investigation.
ex: The quarterly financial report highlighted record user acquisition and steady revenue growth worldwide.
nat: According to official weather reports, a tropical storm is approaching the southern coast.

mis.bad: I wrote a report about the problems.
mis.good: I wrote a report on the problems.
mis.why: While "about" is acceptable, "report on [a topic]" is preferred in formal professional contexts.

def: Deserving censure, condemnation, or sharp reprimand; blameworthy.
ex: Falsifying clinical medical trial data for commercial profit is an utterly reprehensible ethical violation.
nat: The committee condemned the executive behavior as morally reprehensible and ordered an audit.

mis.bad: His action was reprehensible of praise.
mis.good: His action was reprehensible and deserving of blame.
mis.why: "Reprehensible" means blameworthy; do not confuse it with "comprehensible" (understandable).

def: A person chosen or appointed to act or speak on behalf of others.
ex: A helpful customer service representative walked me through the account password recovery procedure.
nat: Elected representatives from thirty democratic nations gathered in Brussels to debate climate targets.

mis.bad: I spoke with the representant of the company.
mis.good: I spoke with the company representative.
mis.why: The English noun is "representative" (or colloquially "rep"), never "representant".

def: To subdue someone or something by force, or restrain an emotional impulse.
ex: Trying to repress difficult emotions often leads to chronic stress and insomnia over time.
nat: The military government used riot police and tear gas to repress peaceful street protests.

mis.bad: He repressed about his anger.
mis.good: He repressed his anger.
mis.why: "Repress" is a transitive verb; omit "about".

def: To produce a copy or representation of something; or generate offspring biologically.
ex: Our quality assurance team was unable to reproduce the crash on Linux test machines.
nat: Many microscopic single-celled organisms reproduce asexually through simple cell division.

mis.bad: I could not reproduce to the bug.
mis.good: I could not reproduce the bug.
mis.why: "Reproduce" is directly transitive in software QA contexts; drop "to".

def: To refuse to accept or be associated with; reject the validity of.
ex: The candidate chose to publicly repudiate extremist groups attempting to endorse her election campaign.
nat: The newly elected government moved to repudiate foreign debt contracted under the previous dictatorship.

mis.bad: She repudiated of the statement.
mis.good: She repudiated the statement.
mis.why: "Repudiate" is a transitive verb; do not insert "of".

def: Extremely distasteful, unacceptable, or repulsive to the senses or morality.
ex: Exploiting vulnerable immigrant workers for cheap factory labor is morally repugnant to society.
nat: The rotten fish emitted a repugnant chemical odor that made the entire kitchen unbreathable.

mis.bad: The food was repugnant of taste.
mis.good: The food had a repugnant taste.
mis.why: Say "had a repugnant taste" or "was repugnant", not "repugnant of taste".

def: To need for a particular purpose, or make necessary as a condition.
ex: Logging into the company internal VPN requires completing multi-factor authentication on your smartphone.
nat: Learning to speak a foreign language fluently requires hundreds of hours of conversational practice.

mis.bad: The job requires to have experience.
mis.good: The job requires experience / requires you to have experience.
mis.why: Use "require + noun" or "require [someone] to + verb", not "require to + verb" with no subject.

def: To have a similar appearance, quality, or character to someone or something.
ex: The architecture of the new cloud platform closely resembles that of its predecessor.
nat: He definitely resembles his maternal grandfather in both facial structure and infectious laughter.

mis.bad: He resembles with his father.
mis.good: He resembles his father.
mis.why: False preposition alert: "resemble" is directly transitive in English; never add "with" or "to".

def: Bitter indignation at having been treated unfairly over a period of time.
ex: Unfair distribution of annual performance bonuses created deep resentment among senior engineering staff.
nat: Holding onto lingering personal resentment only harms your own emotional and physical well-being.

mis.bad: He has resentment with his boss.
mis.good: He harbors resentment toward his boss.
mis.why: Use "resentment toward/against [someone]", not "with".

def: To have one's permanent home in a particular place.
ex: Digital nomads must check tax treaties if they reside in Portugal for six months.
nat: The ultimate authority to approve strategic acquisitions resides solely with the company board.

mis.bad: He resides at São Paulo.
mis.good: He resides in São Paulo.
mis.why: Use "reside in [a city/country]", not "at".

def: A person's home; the place where someone lives, especially an official one.
ex: The French ambassador hosted a welcoming reception at his official residence in Brasília.
nat: Foreign remote contractors must provide proof of residence when opening local bank accounts.

mis.bad: I live in a big residence.
mis.good: I live in a large house / residence.
mis.why: "Residence" is formal or legal; in everyday conversation, say "home", "house", or "apartment".

def: A person who lives somewhere on a long-term basis, or a doctor in training.
ex: Local residents petitioned the municipal council to install speed bumps near the elementary school.
nat: The hospital pediatric ward relies on skilled first-year medical residents during night shifts.

mis.bad: The residents of the hotel complained.
mis.good: The hotel guests complained.
mis.why: For hotels, use "guests", not "residents" (which refers to permanent or long-term inhabitants).

def: To withstand the action or effect of, or try to prevent by action.
ex: It is nearly impossible to resist eating freshly baked warm chocolate chip cookies.
nat: The body immune system works around the clock to resist viral and bacterial pathogens.

mis.bad: I cannot resist to eat dessert.
mis.good: I cannot resist eating dessert.
mis.why: Always use "resist + -ing" (gerund) or a direct noun object, never "resist to + base verb".

def: The refusal to accept or comply with something; or opposition offered by a substance.
ex: Management encountered stiff resistance from staff when announcing mandatory return-to-office office policies.
nat: Aerodynamic resistance increases quadratically as an automobile travels at higher freeway speeds.

mis.bad: The plan met with many resistances.
mis.good: The plan met with strong resistance.
mis.why: "Resistance" is uncountable in the sense of opposition; use "strong resistance", not plural "resistances".

def: Opposed to something and wanting to prevent it; or not damaged by something.
ex: The new smartphone features a scratch-resistant glass screen and water-resistant protective seals.
nat: Senior executives are often resistant to adopting open-source tooling over expensive proprietary software.

mis.bad: He is resistant with the new proposal.
mis.good: He is resistant to the new proposal.
mis.why: The preposition after "resistant" is always "to", never "with".

def: To produce or be filled with a deep, full, reverberating sound; or evoke positive emotional response.
ex: Her heartfelt talk on mental wellness resonated deeply with software engineers in the auditorium.
nat: The acoustic guitar wooden body is specially constructed to resonate warmly when strummed.

mis.bad: His message resonated to the audience.
mis.good: His message resonated with the audience.
mis.why: The correct idiom is "resonate with [someone]", not "to".

def: To turn to and adopt a strategy or course of action, especially an unpleasant one.
ex: Engineers should never resort to monkey-patching production code when proper architectural refactoring is needed.
nat: The frustrated travelers had to resort to sleeping on airport benches overnight.

mis.bad: We resorted in using old backups.
mis.good: We resorted to using old backups.
mis.why: Always use "resort to + [noun / -ing]", never "resort in".

def: A feeling of deep admiration for someone or something; or a particular aspect or detail.
ex: Treating junior developers with patience and genuine respect fosters an extraordinary engineering culture.
nat: In this respect, the newly proposed architecture is vastly superior to the legacy solution.

mis.bad: I have much respect by him.
mis.good: I have great respect for him.
mis.why: Have respect "for" someone, not "by".

def: Feeling or showing deference, esteem, and polite regard for others.
ex: Maintain a calm and respectful tone even when challenging an architectural decision in reviews.
nat: The foreign tourists were quiet and respectful while touring the historic Buddhist temple.

mis.bad: He was very respectful with the elders.
mis.good: He was very respectful toward the elders.
mis.why: Say "respectful to / toward [someone]", not "with".

def: Belonging or relating separately to each of two or more people or things.
ex: After the general conference keynote, participants dispersed to their respective breakout workshop rooms.
nat: Both teams submitted their respective quarterly budget proposals to the finance committee yesterday.

mis.bad: Each person went to your respective room.
mis.good: Each person went to their respective room.
mis.why: Use "their respective" when referring back to indefinite singular subjects like "each person".

def: Singly in the order mentioned (used when matching two parallel lists).
ex: Ana and Lucas scored ninety-five and ninety-eight on the technical exam, respectively.
nat: The revenue figures for June and July were ten and twelve million dollars, respectively.

mis.bad: They earned 10 and 20 dollars in respective.
mis.good: They earned 10 and 20 dollars, respectively.
mis.why: Use the adverb "respectively" at the end of the clause, set off with a comma.

def: A person who replies to something, especially one supplying information for a survey.
ex: Over seventy percent of survey respondents reported preferring hybrid remote work schedules.
nat: The court summoned the legal respondent to present evidence within thirty business days.

mis.bad: The responder of the survey answered.
mis.good: The survey respondent answered.
mis.why: For survey participants, use "respondent", not "responder" (which usually means an emergency first responder).

def: The restoration of something lost or stolen to its proper owner; or compensation.
ex: The judge ordered the convicted fraudster to pay full financial restitution to all victims.
nat: Museums across Europe face growing pressure to arrange the restitution of looted colonial artifacts.

mis.bad: He made a restitution of the money.
mis.good: He made restitution for the stolen money.
mis.why: "Restitution" is typically uncountable: "make restitution for [damage/theft]".

def: To replenish a store or supply with fresh stock or supplies.
ex: Supermarket staff worked through the night to restock grocery shelves before the holiday rush.
nat: We need to restock our office coffee beans and oat milk supplies by tomorrow.

mis.bad: They restocked of the shelves.
mis.good: They restocked the shelves.
mis.why: "Restock" is directly transitive; omit "of".

def: To prevent someone or something from doing something; keep under control.
ex: Security guards had to physically restrain the aggressive protestor from entering the stage.
nat: Try to restrain your spending impulses during major annual online shopping discount events.

mis.bad: He restrained himself of speaking.
mis.good: He restrained himself from speaking.
mis.why: Use "restrain [someone] from + -ing", never "of".

def: Unemotional, self-controlled, or moderate behavior; or a device limiting movement.
ex: The diplomat exercised remarkable emotional restraint during the hostile television debate interview.
nat: Always ensure child passenger safety restraints are properly secured before driving on highways.

mis.bad: He showed much restrain in the meeting.
mis.good: He showed great restraint in the meeting.
mis.why: Use the noun "restraint", not the verb "restrain".

def: A limiting condition or measure, especially a legal or regulatory rule.
ex: The municipal government lifted pandemic travel restrictions following a sharp drop in hospitalizations.
nat: There is a strict fifteen-kilogram weight restriction on all domestic passenger carry-on luggage.

mis.bad: There are restrictions of speed on this road.
mis.good: There are speed restrictions on this road.
mis.why: Use noun adjuncts like "speed restrictions" or "restrictions on [speed/travel]".

def: Imposing restrictions on someone's activities, freedom, or choices.
ex: The software company non-compete clause was criticized as unfairly restrictive for departing engineers.
nat: Living under an overly restrictive diet often triggers binge eating and unhealthy guilt cycles.

mis.bad: The law is very restrict.
mis.good: The law is very restrictive.
mis.why: The English adjective is "restrictive", not "restrict" (which is a verb).

def: To begin to do or pursue something again after a pause or interruption.
ex: Let us take a fifteen-minute coffee break and resume the presentation at three.
nat: The commuter train will resume normal weekday service starting early next Monday morning.

mis.bad: Can you resume the meeting for me? (meaning summarize)
mis.good: Can you summarize the meeting for me?
mis.why: False friend alert: "resume" in English means restart/continue after a pause; to make a summary, use "summarize".

def: An increase or revival after a period of little activity, popularity, or occurrence.
ex: Vinyl records have experienced a remarkable global commercial resurgence among young music collectors.
nat: Public health authorities warned of a potential seasonal resurgence of influenza this winter.

mis.bad: There is a resurgency of interest in chess.
mis.good: There is a resurgence of interest in chess.
mis.why: The correct noun form is "resurgence", not "resurgency".

def: To restore a dead person to life; or revive something forgotten or disused.
ex: The product team decided to resurrect an old design prototype that users had loved.
nat: Archaeologists strived to resurrect the lost ancient language using carved stone tablet inscriptions.

mis.bad: They resurrected up the old idea.
mis.good: They resurrected the old idea.
mis.why: Do not add "up" to "resurrect"; it is directly transitive.

def: To make an attack or assault in return for a similar attack.
ex: The company chose not to retaliate with aggressive price cuts against the rival startup.
nat: If employees report safety hazards, it is illegal for employers to retaliate against them.

mis.bad: They retaliated to the competitor.
mis.good: They retaliated against the competitor.
mis.why: Use "retaliate against [someone]", not "retaliate to".

def: The action of returning a military attack or harmful action; revenge.
ex: Whistleblower protection laws shield employees from corporate retaliation when reporting internal financial fraud.
nat: The rival brand launched negative television commercials in direct retaliation for our campaign.

mis.bad: He acted in retaliation against of the tweet.
mis.good: He acted in retaliation for the tweet.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "in retaliation for [an offense]", not "against of".

def: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved in speech.
ex: The senior systems architect was reticent about discussing ongoing confidential research and development.
nat: She felt unusually reticent during her first few technical video meetings in English.

mis.bad: He was reticent to talk (meaning reluctant).
mis.good: He was reluctant to talk / reticent about the issue.
mis.why: Note: "reticent" strictly means quiet or uncommunicative; do not confuse it with "reluctant" (unwilling).

def: A person who has retired from employment or professional service.
ex: Many active retirees volunteer their weekend time teaching literacy classes at community libraries.
nat: The coastal resort town attracts thousands of affluent retirees seeking warm year-round sunshine.

mis.bad: My grandfather is a retired.
mis.good: My grandfather is a retiree / is retired.
mis.why: Use the noun "retiree" or the predicate adjective "is retired", never "a retired".

def: An act of coming or going back; or profit on an investment.
ex: Diversified index funds typically offer a solid annualized return on investment over decades.
nat: We booked a round-trip ticket that includes a direct evening return to Lisbon.

mis.bad: The project gave a good return of money.
mis.good: The project gave a good financial return.
mis.why: Say "a good financial return" or "return on investment", not "return of money".

def: To give new and improved form, structure, or appearance to something.
ex: The engineering organization decided to revamp its entire onboarding process for remote engineers.
nat: Marketing hired an external creative agency to revamp the corporate branding and typography.

mis.bad: We revamped up our homepage.
mis.good: We revamped our homepage.
mis.why: "Revamp" is directly transitive; do not add "up".

def: To return to a previous state, practice, topic, or condition.
ex: If the deployment fails during verification, our script will automatically revert all changes.
nat: After the power surge subsided, the air conditioning unit reverted to default settings.

mis.bad: Please revert back to the old version.
mis.good: Please revert to the old version.
mis.why: Avoid saying "revert back"; "revert" already means go back, making "back" redundant.

def: To put an end to the validity or operation of a decree, license, or access.
ex: Security administrators must immediately revoke building badge access when an employee departs permanently.
nat: The state authorities moved to revoke his driver license after repeated reckless offenses.

mis.bad: The police revoked of his license.
mis.good: The police revoked his license.
mis.why: "Revoke" is a transitive verb; omit "of".

def: An attempt to put an end to the authority of a person or body by rebelling.
ex: High bread prices and chronic unemployment sparked a violent street revolt in the capital.
nat: Shareholders staged a revolt and rejected the board executive compensation package yesterday afternoon.

mis.bad: The citizens made a revolt against taxes.
mis.good: The citizens staged a revolt against taxes.
mis.why: Use verbs like "stage / lead / crush a revolt", not "make a revolt".

def: The art of effective or persuasive speaking or writing; or insincere language.
ex: Behind the polished campaign rhetoric lay very few realistic and actionable legislative proposals.
nat: Studying classical rhetoric helps public speakers structure persuasive arguments for diverse audiences.

mis.bad: His speech was full of retorics.
mis.good: His speech was full of empty rhetoric.
mis.why: "Rhetoric" is uncountable in English; do not pluralize it as "retorics".

def: The quality of being rich, detailed, flavorful, or deeply interesting.
ex: I was captivated by the sheer richness and diversity of Amazonian wildlife species.
nat: The slow-cooked mushroom stew had an incredible depth and savory culinary richness.

mis.bad: The richness of him was famous.
mis.good: His wealth was famous.
mis.why: Use "wealth" when referring to money; use "richness" for quality, texture, detail, or flavor.

def: A person who rides a horse, bicycle, or motorcycle; or an added contract clause.
ex: Every motorcycle rider must wear an approved protective helmet under local transportation laws.
nat: The insurance policy includes a special optional rider covering international medical emergencies.

mis.bad: The rider of the bike fell.
mis.good: The bicycle rider fell off.
mis.why: Use "bicycle rider / cyclist" directly as a compound or single noun.

def: A long, narrow hilltop, mountain range, or elevated narrow strip.
ex: Hikers walked along the narrow mountain ridge with breathtaking panoramic views on both sides.
nat: High-pressure atmospheric ridges often bring extended periods of clear skies and sunny weather.

mis.bad: We walked on the crista of the hill.
mis.good: We walked along the ridge of the hill.
mis.why: Remember "ridge" is the English word for mountain "crista".

def: To change the position or direction of something slightly, especially goals or resources.
ex: The leadership team met offsite to realign company quarterly goals with current market realities.
nat: You should have a mechanic realign your car wheels if the vehicle pulls sideways.

mis.bad: We realigned with the priorities.
mis.good: We realigned our priorities.
mis.why: "Realign" takes a direct object without "with" when referring to goals or resources.
